**Lamport timestamps** [1] assign a single logical number to every event per process. If the vectors are not comparable element-wise, the events were concurrent. [1]

legacy.answer:
False sharing is a performance problem that occurs in multicore systems when two processors operate on independent data that happens to occupy the same cache line [1]. A cache line is the smallest unit of memory that the caching system manages, typically 64 bytes [2].

Here is why it degrades performance. Cache coherence protocols like MESI maintain consistency across cores by tracking the state of each cache line in each core's cache [2]. When one core writes to a cache line that another core also has cached, the hardware must invalidate the other core's copy and force it to re-fetch the entire cache line on its next access [2]. This happens even though the two cores are modifying completely different variables that just happen to sit in the same 64-byte block [2].

The result is severe. Two threads that logically operate on unrelated data are forced to run nearly serially because they keep invalidating each other's cache lines [2]. A concrete example shows the cost: two threads each incrementing their own counter 100 million times, with no logical sharing between them, runs about 20 times slower when both counters fit in a single cache line than when each occupies its own line [2]. In some cases, eliminating false sharing can yield order-of-magnitude performance improvements [1].

The fix is to pad variables with unused space so that independent data lands on separate cache lines [1]. For instance, using `alignas(64)` in C++ ensures each variable gets its own cache line [2]. False sharing is invisible to correctness checking tools like TSan or ASan because there is no actual data race or undefined behavior; the code is logically correct but mysteriously slow [2].

When one core writes to a cache line that another core also has cached, the hardware must invalidate the other core's copy and force it to re-fetch the entire cache line on its next access [2]. This happens even though the two cores are modifying completely different variables that just happen to sit in the same 64-byte block [2].

The result is severe. Two threads that logically operate on unrelated data are forced to run nearly serially because they keep invalidating each other's cache lines [2]. A concrete example shows the cost: two threads each incrementing their own counter 100 million times, with no logical sharing between them, runs about 20 times slower when both counters fit in a single cache line than when each occupies its own line [2]. In some cases, eliminating false sharing can yield order-of-magnitude performance improvements [1].

The fix is to pad variables with unused space so that independent data lands on separate cache lines [1]. For instance, using `alignas(64)` in C++ ensures each variable gets its own cache line [2]. False sharing is invisible to correctness checking tools like TSan or ASan because there is no actual data race or undefined behavior; the code is logically correct but mysteriously slow [2].

The key problem: the granularity of coherence is the entire cache line, not individual variables, so logically unrelated data can trigger this invalidation cascade [2].

The performance impact is severe. Two threads incrementing independent counters on the same cache line can be 15 to 50 times slower than when those counters occupy separate cache lines [2]. The code looks parallel and contains no logical data races, but the cores effectively run serially as they keep invalidating each other's cache copies [2]. This is particularly insidious because standard correctness tools like TSan or ASan won't catch it; only performance profilers reveal the problem [2].
